comparator.name: Liberal Arts and Sciences: Global Challenges
comparator.institution: Leiden University College The Hague, Leiden University
comparator.sourceNotes: The live 2026–27 Leiden product confirms a 180-EC degree: 45 EC first-year compulsory study, an 85-EC major, 10 EC electives, 30 EC minor/semester abroad/electives and 10 EC Global Citizenship. The generic target has six formal majors. CHS is selected before UCR fit as the broadest humanities-and-social-science expression of the generic interdisciplinary identity. The component list spans current CHS cultural-expression, historical-process and social-forms courses, its research-methods progression and 10-EC capstone; it selects Mathematics for Social Networks from the mathematics options and Spanish Beginners as a complete current Global Citizenship option. Genuine flexible space stays explicit. Every component is counted once and totals 180 EC.

routeSelection.basis: The normalized target names the generic degree, not one major. The official product lists six majors. CHS combines humanities and social sciences across culture, history, politics, society, difference and research and is the least narrowly disciplinary expression of the broad identity; it is selected before UCR course search.

core: Interdisciplinary analysis of global challenges and complex problems from multiple perspectives
Living together across cultures, histories and societies, with cross-cultural communication and global citizenship
Collective action, social difference, inequality, culture and the organisation of social life
Research design, qualitative and quantitative inquiry, data analysis and ethical reflection
Climate change, Earth systems, energy transitions, environmental sustainability and resource governance
Governance, economics, development and public institutions in addressing global problems
Human rights, international law and justice across borders
World politics, peace, conflict, security and international relations
adjacent: Earth, Energy and Sustainability as a formal LUC major direction
Governance, Economics and Development as a formal LUC major direction
International Justice as a formal LUC major direction
World Politics as a formal LUC major direction
questions: How can people respond to climate change and live together on a finite planet?
How do culture, historical power and social difference shape global citizenship and collective action?
How can institutions, law and international politics address inequality, conflict and development?

alternatives.label: Culture, History and Society in Global Perspective
alternatives.labelReason: The 24 courses combine modern and imperial history, sociology, politics, literature, media, communication and qualitative research. The label names these strands and their global perspective without presenting them as Leiden’s named major.
alternatives.concept: An interdisciplinary humanities and social-science programme examining how cultures, histories, institutions and forms of social difference shape collective life and global challenges, with qualitative and historical research throughout.
progression: Formal prerequisites and Fall-2026-cohort offerings were checked against the enriched workbook. PPD is in Year 1; foundations precede advanced theory, politics, media and research; all 24 courses are unique and eight are level 300.

alternatives.label: Earth Systems, Sustainability and Environmental Economics
alternatives.labelReason: Earth and environmental science, water, ecology, sustainability and resource governance dominate, with economics, data and quantitative methods supporting environmental decisions.
alternatives.concept: A science-and-policy route for understanding climate, Earth systems, biodiversity, water, energy and resource transitions, combining environmental research with economics, data analysis and sustainability governance.
alternatives.distinctness: Fourteen courses differ in each direction from the closest CHS programme. Earth and environmental gateways, GIS, hydrology, ecology, climate, resource science, economics and sustainability research replace much of the historical, literary, media and social-theory curriculum.
progression: Formal prerequisites and fixed cohort offerings were checked. Earth, sustainability, economics, mathematics and data foundations precede GIS, hydrology, resource analysis, upper-level research and governance; PPD is in Year 1 and eight courses are level 300.

alternatives.label: Global Politics, Justice and Political Economy
alternatives.labelReason: The curriculum centres political theory, comparative politics, international relations, law, economics and security, with history, sociology, research and public communication as supporting disciplines.
alternatives.concept: A governance-centred route addressing global inequality, development, institutions, international law, human rights, conflict and political economy through political science, law, economics and social research.
alternatives.distinctness: Thirteen courses differ in each direction from CHS and twenty from Earth and Sustainability. Political economy, legal institutions, human rights and international security become the organising core.
progression: Formal prerequisites and fixed cohort offerings were checked. Gateways precede international, constitutional and EU law, public economics, econometrics, EU politics and peace and conflict. PPD is in Year 1 and eight courses are level 300.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

Examines consumer and producer behaviour, uncertainty and market structures, giving the political-economy route tools for analysing incentives
Analyses taxation, public goods and externalities to assess how governments pursue efficiency and equity
Teaches regression, causal inference and prediction for testing economic claims about policy and development
Introduces research design, operationalisation and statistics needed to assess social and economic evidence
Teaches data cleaning and visualisation, including spatial data, for investigating environmental evidence
Provides calculus and linear algebra needed for quantitative analysis of environmental systems
Develops probability, distributions, estimation and simulation to assess environmental uncertainty
Studies ecosystem-based design for flood protection, land reclamation and port development as an adaptation response
Examines sea-level rise, freshwater scarcity, subsidence and unequal flood protection through delta water-management projects
Investigates recycling, resource recovery and remediation technologies that support a circular economy
Analyses how government and other actors make sustainability rules and collective resource decisions
Introduces biodiversity and ecological pressures that shape conservation and finite-planet decisions
Introduces interacting Earth systems and cycles through laboratory and field study, grounding the environmental route
Uses geoscience to compare natural and climate-related hazards and evaluate risk reduction and adaptation
Uses satellite and drone images with GIS to investigate human impacts on ecosystems and climate

Analyses interactions among water, rocks, soils and minerals and their implications for pollution and resource cycles
Investigates geothermal energy, carbon storage and nuclear-waste problems through geoscience research
Builds the physics, chemistry, materials and modelling foundation for later sustainability and environmental courses
Applies the first sustainability gateway’s scientific tools to a concrete sustainability case before advanced work
Examines anthropogenic climate drivers, sea-level and ecological effects, and mitigation and adaptation options
Requires a team research project on a delta sustainability problem, joining methods to a local environmental application
Introduces legal, social and normative perspectives on law and justice before the specialised rights and institutions sequence
Traces industrialisation, sovereignty and social change from 1815 onward as historical context for global challenges
Examines imperial power and its contested legacies, informing the routes on historical inequality and world order
Traces warfare, strategy and military technology to historicise conflict and security in the governance route
Studies Indigenous histories, colonial violence and resilience to analyse power and social difference across societies
Develops primary-source historical inquiry in a substantial research paper, supporting the culture-and-history route’s method
Connects human-rights treaties and cases with philosophical arguments about liberty and equality
Studies treaties, the UN, armed conflict and refugee protection as international rules for cross-border problems
Compares constitutional design, separation of powers and judicial review to analyse state authority and rights
Studies EU institutions, citizenship and the internal market as a specific supranational legal order
Applies virtue ethics, duties and consequences to contested responsibilities in collective life
Examines authority, freedom, equality and democracy as normative foundations for public institutions
Compares political systems, parties, populism and democratic backsliding to explain institutional variation
Applies international-relations theories to war, climate, energy and intervention across states
Studies EU actors, institutions and decision rules in responses to regional crises
Analyses violence, radicalisation, reconciliation and conflict transformation for peace-oriented governance
Introduces sociological concepts and classic theories for examining inequality and social organisation
Teaches qualitative questions, interpretation and small-team field inquiry into complex social relations
Connects modern social theory with imperialism and colonial responses to explain social difference
Uses environmental-justice cases and movement theories to examine unequal exposure and collective responses
Examines civil society, decolonial critique and NGO research projects as advanced analysis of collective action
Studies rhetoric in speeches, protests and public messages to analyse and practise civic communication
Builds practical Dutch oral and written communication for participation in local cross-cultural settings
Applies framing, persuasion and ethical communication to public challenges, including sustainability organisations
Investigates creative writing, performance and sonic forms as ways cultures construct and share meaning
Studies ancient craft objects across world regions to investigate how material production shapes identity
Introduces analysis of fiction, poetry, drama and film as forms through which societies construct meaning
Reads literary traditions from Gilgamesh to modernity to compare representations of belonging and human experience
Compares literary and film narratives, adaptation and intertextuality to study cultural representation
Examines visual depictions of the Anthropocene and contested nature in environmental media
Studies race and power in film, photography and podcasts, including whose histories are remembered or erased

candidates.label: Global governance, justice and world politics

selection.assessment: After the broad CHS response, two generator-backed formal directions pass coherence, feasibility and pairwise distinctness: Earth, Energy and Sustainability; and a governance cluster combining Governance, Economics and Development, International Justice and World Politics. All direct and stable interests are owned by the core or these candidates, and the maximum of three alternatives is reached.

notes.text: Leiden embeds an 85-EC named major, prescribed research methods and a 10-EC capstone within a residential honours-college programme. UCR can assemble rigorous interdisciplinary 180-EC curricula, but these are illustrative compositions rather than official LUC majors and do not reproduce the residential structure or required capstone.
